# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.
- If you are updating or improving an artifact that already exists, re-use its same `id` so that your new version replaces the old one rather than creating a duplicate.

## Never allowed — always stripped, even if instructed
<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.
<a href> to external sites is fine. Inline data: image URIs are fine.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

You can switch between different modes using the switch_mode tool. Each mode provides access to different capabilities and tools optimized for specific types of tasks.

**When to switch modes:**
- The user explicitly requests a mode switch
- You need a tool that is ONLY available in another mode and is absolutely required to complete the task

**DO NOT switch modes when:**
- You can accomplish the task with your current tools
- The request is ambiguous

Stay in your current mode unless there is an explicit, compelling reason to switch. When in doubt, do not switch.

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

For factual questions that require knowledge about IBM products, platforms, languages, commands, APIs, configuration, documented behavior, compatibility, or product-specific errors, consult IBM documentation before answering.
This includes technologies such as IBM i, IBM Z, z/OS, Db2, CICS, COBOL, JCL, RPG, AIX, and watsonx, even when the user does not explicitly say IBM.
For Bob(or IBM Bob) product questions, call `search_ibm_docs` directly with `library_name: "bob"`.
For other IBM products, first call `list_ibm_doc_libraries`, select the most relevant exact library name from its response, and then call `search_ibm_docs`. Do not invent or modify library names.
You may reuse a library name already returned in the current conversation for follow-up questions about the same product.
Base factual product claims on the retrieved documentation. If no suitable library or relevant documentation is found, say so rather than guessing.
Documentation lookup is unnecessary when the request is purely about code in the workspace and does not require IBM product knowledge.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

Available types:
- "explore": Explore codebase (read tools, explorer model)
- "general": Inherits current mode tools, default model

**fork_context**: Set to true when the subagent needs to understand prior conversation — e.g., decisions made, constraints discovered, or user preferences expressed earlier.
Leave false (default) when the description alone is sufficient context.

Do NOT use subagents for:
- Simple file reads, searches, or single-tool operations
- Tasks where you already have relevant context
- Quick lookups that would take fewer turns done directly

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

## ThirdEye AI — Frontend/Backend Integration Plan

### Current State Summary

The frontend is **more complete than expected**. All pages have already been migrated away from mock data to live API calls. The service layer (`client.js`, `projects.js`, `reviews.js`, `findings.js`, `tests.js`) is correctly wired to `http://localhost:8080`. No files need a wholesale rewrite — only targeted fixes.

---

### CORS — ⚠️ Critical Gap

**Problem:** All four backend controllers use `@CrossOrigin(origins = "${thirdeye.cors.allowed-origins:http://localhost:5174}")`. The property placeholder fallback defaults to port **5174**, and the resolved value from `application.properties` is a comma-separated string — **which `@CrossOrigin` does not split**. The Vite dev server runs on **5173** by default. Any port mismatch causes every API call to be blocked by the browser before it even reaches the backend.

- **File:** [`src/main/resources/application.properties`](src/main/resources/application.properties) — CORS origins already lists all ports 5173–5176 ✅  
- **File:** [`src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/ProjectController.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/ProjectController.java) — `@CrossOrigin` uses a single `origins` string from the property; Spring parses it correctly when the property is a comma-separated value only if `@CrossOrigin` maps to a `String[]`. The current form `origins = "${…}"` resolves to a single string, **not an array**. Spring Boot's annotation processor does handle comma-separated strings in this position, but a centralized `WebMvcConfigurer` bean is the only guaranteed-correct approach.  
- **Action needed:** Replace all per-controller `@CrossOrigin` annotations with a single `WebMvcConfigurer` CORS bean in a new `CorsConfig.java`, reading `thirdeye.cors.allowed-origins` as a `List<String>`.

---

### Issue Map by File — Prioritized

#### Priority 1 — Backend: CORS configuration (blocks everything)

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| New: `src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/CorsConfig.java` | Add a `WebMvcConfigurer` bean that reads the comma-separated `thirdeye.cors.allowed-origins` property into a `String[]` and registers it for `/api/**` |
| `ProjectController.java`, `ReviewController.java`, `FindingController.java`, `TestController.java` | Remove `@CrossOrigin` annotation from each — handled by the global config |

---

#### Priority 2 — Frontend: `triggerAnalysis` missing from `reviews.js`

**Problem:** The `ReviewController` exposes `POST /api/reviews/{id}/analyze`. The `Overview` page has a "Re-trigger" path for FAILED reviews that navigates to `/dashboard/diff` instead of calling the API. There is no `triggerAnalysis` export in [`src/services/api/reviews.js`](src/services/api/reviews.js).

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `src/services/api/reviews.js` | Add `export const triggerAnalysis = (reviewId) => apiRequest(...)` |
| `src/pages/Overview.jsx` | Wire the "Re-trigger" button on the FAILED banner to call `triggerAnalysis(review.id)` and restart the polling loop |

---

#### Priority 3 — Frontend: `Findings.jsx` category filter mismatch

**Problem:** The Findings page filter has hardcoded categories `['All', 'Security', 'Quality', 'Style']`. The backend `MockAnalysisService` writes categories in **lowercase**: `"security"`, `"quality"`, `"bugs"`, `"coverage"`. The filter compares `f.category?.toLowerCase() === category.toLowerCase()` which handles the case-conversion — **but `"bugs"` and `"coverage"` are never in the filter list**, so those findings are invisible unless "All" is selected.

| File | Change |
|---|---|
| `src/pages/Findings.jsx` | Replace the static `categories` array with `['All', 'Security', 'Bugs', 'Quality', 'Coverage']` (matching the mock engine's actual output) |

+package com.thirdeye.backend;
+
+import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
+import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
+import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.CorsRegistry;
+import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.WebMvcConfigurer;
+
+import java.util.List;
+
+/**
+ * Centralised CORS configuration for all /api/** endpoints.
+ *
+ * Reads the comma-separated list of allowed origins from
+ * thirdeye.cors.allowed-origins (application.properties) so the
+ * four controllers no longer need individual @CrossOrigin annotations.
+ *
+ * Wildcard origins are intentionally NOT used because the frontend
+ * sends no credentials; however, the explicit origin list keeps
+ * the configuration forward-compatible if credentials are added later.
+ */
+@Configuration
+public class CorsConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
+
+    /** Injected as a List — Spring splits the comma-separated property automatically. */
+    @Value("${thirdeye.cors.allowed-origins}")
+    private List<String> allowedOrigins;
+
+    @Override
+    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
+        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
+                .allowedOrigins(allowedOrigins.toArray(String[]::new))
+                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE", "OPTIONS")
+                .allowedHeaders("*")
+                .allowCredentials(false)
+                .maxAge(3600);
+    }
+}

## Root Cause Analysis

There are **two compounding causes**, not one:

### Cause 1 — `@RestControllerAdvice` intercepts the H2 console's own error path

[`GlobalExceptionHandler.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler.java) registers a catch-all `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` handler on a `@RestControllerAdvice` bean **with no package restriction**. This means it intercepts exceptions thrown by **every servlet** in the application context — including the H2 console servlet, which is a plain `javax.servlet.Servlet` registered under `/h2-console/**` by Spring Boot's `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration`.

When the browser hits `/h2-console` for the first time, the H2 console servlet normally redirects to `/h2-console/login.jsp`. If anything in that dispatch chain throws (e.g. a missing init resource, an unresolved view, or simply the fact that the H2 console uses `HttpServletResponse.sendRedirect()` which bypasses Spring MVC — but the forward/error dispatch hits the `DispatcherServlet` error path), the `handleGeneric` handler converts it to a `500 {"message": "An unexpected error occurred..."}` JSON response before the browser can receive the redirect or the HTML login page.

### Cause 2 — The `GlobalExceptionHandler` has no restriction on media type or path

`@RestControllerAdvice` without `basePackages`, `assignableTypes`, or `annotations` restrictions applies globally. The H2 console's servlet path `/h2-console/**` is served by a separate `ServletRegistrationBean`, but error dispatches from that path can still be caught by the `DispatcherServlet`'s `HandlerExceptionResolver` chain, which includes `@ControllerAdvice` beans.

### The fix

Restrict `@RestControllerAdvice` to **only** handle exceptions from the application's own controllers by scoping it to the `com.thirdeye.backend.controller` package. This is the minimal safe change — it leaves all `@RestController` error handling intact and stops the handler from intercepting H2 console traffic.

No security config, no `spring-security` dependency, no database changes, no `application.properties` changes are needed.

## Root Cause & Fix — Full Report

### What was happening

The `@RestControllerAdvice` in [`GlobalExceptionHandler.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler.java) had **no scope restriction**. By default, `@RestControllerAdvice` (and `@ControllerAdvice`) applies to **all controllers and servlet dispatches** in the Spring MVC context — including the H2 console servlet registered by `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration`.

When the browser requests `/h2-console` (no trailing slash), the H2 console servlet attempts an internal forward/redirect to `/h2-console/login.jsp`. Depending on how the servlet container dispatches this (particularly with Spring Boot 4.x / embedded Tomcat), any exception thrown during that dispatch — including something as minor as a `NoHandlerFoundException` or a response-commit race — was caught by the unrestricted catch-all:

```java
@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
public ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> handleGeneric(Exception ex) {
    return build(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "An unexpected error occurred...");
}
```

This intercepted the response **before** the H2 console's own HTML could be written, replacing it with the generic JSON 500.

There is **no Spring Security** in this project, so no security config was involved.

### The single-line fix

**File changed:** [`src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/exception/GlobalExceptionHandler.java)

```diff
-@RestControllerAdvice
+@RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.thirdeye.backend.controller")
```

The `basePackages` attribute restricts exception handling to controllers inside `com.thirdeye.backend.controller` only. The H2 console, error pages, and any other non-API servlets are excluded. All four REST controllers (`ProjectController`, `ReviewController`, `FindingController`, `TestController`) remain fully covered.

### Build result

```
Tests run: 16, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0 — BUILD SUCCESS
```

I have 100% confirmed the root cause. Now I'll fix the `pom.xml`:

---

## Root Cause

**Spring Boot 4.0 removed `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration` from `spring-boot-autoconfigure`** and moved it into a new standalone module: `org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-h2console`. The `spring-boot-autoconfigure-4.1.1.jar` contains only 12 auto-configurations (none related to H2, JDBC, JPA, or data) — **the entire data tier was extracted into separate modules in the 4.x rewrite**.

The `spring.h2.console.enabled=true` property is read correctly, but because `spring-boot-h2console` is not on the classpath, `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration` never runs, no servlet is registered under `/h2-console`, and the request returns 404.

**The fix is one `<dependency>` block in `pom.xml`.**

## Root Cause & Fix — Complete Report

### What actually caused the 404

**Spring Boot 4.0 removed `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration` from `spring-boot-autoconfigure` entirely.** It was extracted into a new standalone module: `org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-h2console`.

This was confirmed by directly inspecting the JAR files in the local Maven cache:

| Spring Boot version | `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration` in `spring-boot-autoconfigure`? |
|---|---|
| 3.2.x, 3.3.x, 3.5.x | ✅ present |
| **4.0.x, 4.1.x** | ❌ **absent — zero H2-related classes** |

Because `spring-boot-h2console` was not listed as a dependency in [`pom.xml`](pom.xml), `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration` never ran, no servlet was ever registered at `/h2-console`, and every request to that path returned 404. The `spring.h2.console.enabled=true` property was read but ignored — there was nothing to act on it.

The `GlobalExceptionHandler` change from the previous fix was correct and remains in place — it prevented the 500 — but the 404 was a completely separate, earlier problem.

### The fix — one `<dependency>` block in [`pom.xml`](pom.xml)

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-h2console</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
```

No version is needed — Spring Boot BOM manages it. `scope: runtime` means it is never visible to your application code; it only activates `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration` at startup.

The existing `com.h2database:h2` dependency (also `runtime`) and all `application.properties` settings are preserved exactly as-is.

### Build result

```
Tests run: 16, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0 — BUILD SUCCESS
```

Now I have everything I need. The app is running (PID 25700 holds the current DB lock). The older DB is locked by something else — likely the H2 console still open in the browser. I have all the entity/schema information from the source code. Here is the complete findings and restoration plan.

---

## Findings Report

### 1. Schema — Exact Table and Column Mapping

Derived directly from the entity source code. No assumptions made.

#### `PROJECTS` table
| Column | JPA field | Type | Constraints |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ID` | `id` | `BIGINT` | PK, `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` |
| `NAME` | `name` | `VARCHAR` | NOT NULL |
| `DESCRIPTION` | `description` | `VARCHAR` | nullable |
| `REPOSITORY_URL` | `repositoryUrl` | `VARCHAR` | nullable |
| `STATUS` | `status` | `VARCHAR` | default `'ACTIVE'` |
| `CREATED_AT` | `createdAt` | `TIMESTAMP` | set at construction |

#### `REVIEWS` table
| Column | JPA field | Type | Constraints |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ID` | `id` | `BIGINT` | PK, `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` |
| `PROJECT_ID` | `project` (FK) | `BIGINT` | NOT NULL, FK → `PROJECTS.ID` |
| `TITLE` | `title` | `VARCHAR` | NOT NULL |
| `STATUS` | `status` | `VARCHAR` | default `'PENDING'` |
| `CODE_DIFF` | `codeDiff` | `VARCHAR(100000)` | nullable |
| `FILES_CHANGED` | `filesChanged` | `INT` | |
| `LINES_ADDED` | `linesAdded` | `INT` | |
| `LINES_REMOVED` | `linesRemoved` | `INT` | |
| `COMMITS` | `commits` | `INT` | |
| `PROGRESS` | `progress` | `INT` | default `0` |
| `CREATED_AT` | `createdAt` | `TIMESTAMP` | set at construction |
| `UPDATED_AT` | `updatedAt` | `TIMESTAMP` | updated by `@PreUpdate` |

> **Hibernate column naming:** Spring Boot / Hibernate's default `SpringImplicitNamingStrategy` converts `camelCase` to `snake_case`, so `codeDiff` → `CODE_DIFF`, `filesChanged` → `FILES_CHANGED`, etc. H2 stores names in upper case by default.

#### `FINDINGS` table
| Column | JPA field | Type | Constraints |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ID` | `id` | `BIGINT` | PK, identity |
| `REVIEW_ID` | `review` (FK) | `BIGINT` | NOT NULL, FK → `REVIEWS.ID` |
| `TITLE` | `title` | `VARCHAR` | NOT NULL |
| `SEVERITY` | `severity` | `VARCHAR` | nullable |
| `CATEGORY` | `category` | `VARCHAR` | nullable |
| `FILE` | `file` | `VARCHAR` | nullable |
| `LINE` | `line` | `INT` | |
| `DESCRIPTION` | `description` | `VARCHAR(5000)` | nullable |
| `SUGGESTION` | `suggestion` | `VARCHAR(5000)` | nullable |

#### `GENERATED_TESTS` table
| Column | JPA field | Type | Constraints |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ID` | `id` | `BIGINT` | PK, identity |
| `REVIEW_ID` | `review` (FK) | `BIGINT` | NOT NULL, FK → `REVIEWS.ID` |
| `NAME` | `name` | `VARCHAR` | NOT NULL |
| `FILE` | `file` | `VARCHAR` | nullable |
| `STATUS` | `status` | `VARCHAR` | default `'PENDING'` |
| `DURATION` | `duration` | `VARCHAR` | nullable |
| `LINKED_FINDING_ID` | `linkedFindingId` | `VARCHAR` | nullable — **this is a VARCHAR, not a FK** |
| `TEST_CODE` | `testCode` | `VARCHAR(10000)` | nullable |

> **Important:** `LINKED_FINDING_ID` in `GeneratedTest` is declared as `private String linkedFindingId` with no `@JoinColumn` or `@ManyToOne`. It is a plain string column holding the finding's numeric ID as text. There is no database-level foreign key constraint on it. This simplifies restoration.

---

### 2. ID Generation Strategy

All four entities use `@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)`. In H2, this maps to `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` (or equivalent). This means:

- H2 maintains an internal sequence/auto-increment counter per table.
- After the restoration inserts, the counter must be advanced past the highest inserted ID, or the next `INSERT` by the application will collide and fail with a primary key violation.
- H2 tracks `IDENTITY` columns using an internal sequence named by the pattern `SYSTEM_SEQUENCE_<hash>` or (in H2 2.x) via the table's built-in identity column — the sequence state is embedded in the column definition, not a named user sequence.

---

### 3. Dependency Graph for Restoration Order

```
PROJECTS (already exist — must NOT be re-inserted)
    └── REVIEWS  (FK: PROJECT_ID → PROJECTS.ID)
           ├── FINDINGS  (FK: REVIEW_ID → REVIEWS.ID)
           └── GENERATED_TESTS  (FK: REVIEW_ID → REVIEWS.ID)
                    └── LINKED_FINDING_ID  (VARCHAR — no FK, just a string)
```

**Restoration order:** `REVIEWS` → `FINDINGS` → `GENERATED_TESTS`

---

### 4. Why Explicit-ID Inserts Are Safe Here

| Factor | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Current REVIEWS count = 0 | ID 1 is free — no collision risk |
| Current FINDINGS count = 0 | ID 1 is free — no collision risk |
| Current GENERATED_TESTS count = 0 | IDs 1 and 2 are free — no collision risk |
| Both databases have the same PROJECTS (ID 1 and ID 2) | FK constraint `PROJECT_ID=2` will resolve correctly |
| `GenerationType.IDENTITY` with explicit `INSERT` | H2 honours explicit ID values when the column is `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` (the `BY DEFAULT` clause means explicit values override the sequence) |
| Identity sequence state after insert | Must be corrected — see step 6 of the plan below |

---

### 5. The Sequence State Problem

After inserting a row with an explicit ID into a `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY` column in H2, the internal sequence counter is **not automatically advanced** to the inserted ID + 1. If the application then inserts a new review (letting H2 auto-generate the next ID), H2 may generate ID 1 again, causing a `Unique index or primary key violation`.

The fix is to manually advance the sequence after the inserts. In H2 2.x this is done with:
```sql
ALTER TABLE REVIEWS ALTER COLUMN ID RESTART WITH 2;
ALTER TABLE FINDINGS ALTER COLUMN ID RESTART WITH 2;
ALTER TABLE GENERATED_TESTS ALTER COLUMN ID RESTART WITH 3;
```
(Each value is `max(inserted_id) + 1`.)

---

### 6. Step-by-Step Non-Destructive Restoration Plan

> **Precondition:** The Spring Boot application must be stopped before executing any SQL. The H2 console in your browser must also be disconnected from the older database. Both `.mv.db` files must be free of locks.

**Step 0 — Back up the current database file before touching anything**
```
Copy-Item C:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-backend\data\thirdeye.mv.db `
          C:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-backend\data\thirdeye.mv.db.backup-before-restore
```

**Step 1 — Open the H2 console at `http://localhost:8080/h2-console`**
Connect to the **current** database:
```
JDBC URL: jdbc:h2:file:C:/Users/sanja/Downloads/thirdeye-backend/data/thirdeye
User: sa    Password: (blank)
```

**Step 2 — Verify the current state before doing anything**
```sql
SELECT 'PROJECTS', COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM PROJECTS
UNION ALL SELECT 'REVIEWS', COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM REVIEWS
UNION ALL SELECT 'FINDINGS', COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM FINDINGS
UNION ALL SELECT 'GENERATED_TESTS', COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM GENERATED_TESTS;
```
Expected: PROJECTS=2, REVIEWS=0, FINDINGS=0, GENERATED_TESTS=0. **Stop if this differs.**

**Step 3 — Verify the foreign key anchor exists**
```sql
SELECT ID, NAME FROM PROJECTS WHERE ID = 2;
```
Expected: `2 | Lost & Found`. **Stop if not found.**

**Step 4 — Read the exact data from the older database**
Open a second H2 console session (or use a different tab) connected to the *older* database and run:
```sql
-- In the OLDER database (thirdeye-backend/thirdeye-backend/data/thirdeye):
SELECT * FROM REVIEWS;
SELECT * FROM FINDINGS;
SELECT * FROM GENERATED_TESTS;
```
Copy every column value you see. Use those exact values in Step 5.

**Step 5 — Insert the records into the current database** *(run in the current DB session)*

First, the review:
```sql
INSERT INTO REVIEWS (
    ID, PROJECT_ID, TITLE, STATUS, CODE_DIFF,
    FILES_CHANGED, LINES_ADDED, LINES_REMOVED, COMMITS,
    PROGRESS, CREATED_AT, UPDATED_AT
) VALUES (
    1, 2, '<title from old DB>', '<status from old DB>', '<code_diff from old DB>',
    <files_changed>, <lines_added>, <lines_removed>, <commits>,
    <progress>, '<created_at from old DB>', '<updated_at from old DB>'
);
```

Then the finding:
```sql
INSERT INTO FINDINGS (
    ID, REVIEW_ID, TITLE, SEVERITY, CATEGORY, FILE, LINE, DESCRIPTION, SUGGESTION
) VALUES (
    1, 1, '<title>', '<severity>', '<category>', '<file>', <line>, '<description>', '<suggestion>'
);
```

Then the two generated tests:
```sql
INSERT INTO GENERATED_TESTS (
    ID, REVIEW_ID, NAME, FILE, STATUS, DURATION, LINKED_FINDING_ID, TEST_CODE
) VALUES (
    1, 1, '<name>', '<file>', '<status>', <duration_or_NULL>, '<linked_finding_id>', '<test_code>'
);

INSERT INTO GENERATED_TESTS (
    ID, REVIEW_ID, NAME, FILE, STATUS, DURATION, LINKED_FINDING_ID, TEST_CODE
) VALUES (
    2, 1, '<name>', '<file>', '<status>', <duration_or_NULL>, '<linked_finding_id_or_NULL>', '<test_code>'
);
```

**Step 6 — Advance the identity sequences**
```sql
ALTER TABLE REVIEWS         ALTER COLUMN ID RESTART WITH 2;
ALTER TABLE FINDINGS        ALTER COLUMN ID RESTART WITH 2;
ALTER TABLE GENERATED_TESTS ALTER COLUMN ID RESTART WITH 3;
```

**Step 7 — Verify the restoration**
```sql
SELECT 'PROJECTS',       COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM PROJECTS
UNION ALL SELECT 'REVIEWS',        COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM REVIEWS
UNION ALL SELECT 'FINDINGS',       COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM FINDINGS
UNION ALL SELECT 'GENERATED_TESTS',COUNT(*), MAX(ID) FROM GENERATED_TESTS;

SELECT r.ID, r.TITLE, r.STATUS, r.PROGRESS, p.NAME AS PROJECT
FROM REVIEWS r JOIN PROJECTS p ON r.PROJECT_ID = p.ID;

SELECT f.ID, f.TITLE, f.SEVERITY, f.CATEGORY FROM FINDINGS f WHERE f.REVIEW_ID = 1;

SELECT gt.ID, gt.NAME, gt.STATUS, gt.LINKED_FINDING_ID FROM GENERATED_TESTS gt WHERE gt.REVIEW_ID = 1;
```

**Step 8 — Test the live API after restart**
After stopping and restarting the Spring Boot application:
```
GET http://localhost:8080/api/projects          → 2 projects
GET http://localhost:8080/api/projects/2/reviews → 1 review (ID 1)
GET http://localhost:8080/api/reviews/1/findings → 1 finding
GET http://localhost:8080/api/reviews/1/tests    → 2 tests
```

---

### 7. Risks and Mitigations

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| `CODE_DIFF` column contains special characters (newlines, quotes) | Use the H2 console's multi-line input; escape single quotes as `''`; or use a `$...$$` dollar-quoted string |
| Older DB still locked when you try to read it | Disconnect from the H2 console browser tab that is connected to the older DB before reading it externally |
| Forgetting to advance the sequence (Step 6) | The first new review submitted through the app will fail with PK violation — easily fixed retroactively with the same `ALTER TABLE … RESTART WITH` command |
| Running inserts while the app is running | The Spring Boot Hikari pool holds an exclusive lock on the current DB file — the H2 console **built into the running app** (`http://localhost:8080/h2-console`) is the correct and safe way to run these inserts while the app is running, since it shares the existing connection pool |

> **Recommendation:** Use the H2 console at `http://localhost:8080/h2-console` (i.e., the one served by the running app) to run Steps 2–6. Do **not** stop the app and then try to connect with an external JDBC tool — that risks lock conflicts. The app-embedded console shares the HikariCP connection pool safely.

What it detects

+ * Lines where a string literal that begins with a SQL keyword + * ({@code SELECT}, {@code INSERT}, {@code UPDATE}, {@code DELETE}, + * {@code MERGE}) is concatenated with a variable or expression using + * {@code +} (Java) or {@code ||} (SQL/Groovy string concat). + * + *

Confidence signal

+ * A match is strengthened when the same line also references + * {@code Statement} (not {@code PreparedStatement}) or executes via + * {@code .execute(} / {@code .executeQuery(}, which indicates the + * concatenated string is actually sent to the database driver. + * + *

Limitations

+ *
    + *
  • Pattern-match only — no data-flow or taint tracking.
    • + *
  • Multi-line query construction is not detected if individual + * lines do not each contain a SQL keyword.
    • + *
  • ORMs (Hibernate HQL, Spring Data JPQL) that use string concat + * may trigger a false positive.
    • + *
+ */ +public class SqlInjectionRule implements AnalysisRule { + + // SQL keyword at the start of a string literal + private static final Pattern SQL_STRING_START = Pattern.compile( + "\"\\s*(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|MERGE)\\b", + Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE); + + // String concatenation operator in the same line + private static final Pattern CONCAT_OP = Pattern.compile("\\+|\\|\\|"); + + // Unsafe execution: plain Statement (not PreparedStatement) or .execute( + private static final Pattern UNSAFE_EXEC = Pattern.compile( + "\\bStatement\\b(?!\\s*\\.\\s*prepare)|" + // Statement but not PreparedStatement + "\\.execute(?:Query|Update|Batch)?\\s*\\(", + Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE); + + @Override + public String ruleId() { return "SQLI-001"; } + + @Override + public String name() { return "SQL Injection via String Concatenation"; } + + @Override + public List analyze(List addedLines) { + List findings = new ArrayList<>(); + + for (DiffLine dl : addedLines) { + String content = dl.getContent(); + boolean hasSqlKeyword = SQL_STRING_START.matcher(content).find(); + boolean hasConcat = CONCAT_OP.matcher(content).find(); + + if (!hasSqlKeyword || !hasConcat) continue; + + boolean hasUnsafeExec = UNSAFE_EXEC.matcher(content).find(); + String severity = hasUnsafeExec ? # ThirdEye AI — Static Analysis Engine (Milestone 1)

## Overview

Milestone 1 replaces the previous mock/placeholder analysis pipeline with a
genuine deterministic static-analysis engine.  The engine examines the
**added lines** of a submitted unified diff using a set of pattern-matching
rules and produces findings that are persisted through the existing
`Finding` entity and REST API.

**What this is NOT**:
- Not an AI or LLM model. No external API calls are made.
- Not a full compiler, parser, or data-flow analyser.
- Does not perform type inference, cross-file analysis, or interprocedural
  taint tracking.

A finding means a pattern matched — it indicates a **potential** issue, not
a confirmed exploitable vulnerability.  Each finding includes the rule ID so
results are traceable.

---

## Architecture

```
ReviewController
    └─> ReviewService.createReview / triggerAnalysis
            └─> MockAnalysisService.analyzeAsync  (@Async)
                    └─> StaticAnalysisEngine.analyze(review, diff)
                            ├─> DiffParser.parse(diff)  → List<DiffLine>
                            ├─> SqlInjectionRule.analyze(lines)
                            ├─> HardcodedCredentialRule.analyze(lines)
                            ├─> DangerousExecutionRule.analyze(lines)
                            └─> UnsafeDeserializationRule.analyze(lines)
                    └─> FindingRepository.saveAll(findings)
```

All new code lives in `com.thirdeye.backend.analysis` and its `rules`
sub-package.  No existing entities, repositories, controllers, or DTOs
were changed.

---

## Supported Rules

| Rule ID   | Title                                | Severity (max) | Category  |
|-----------|--------------------------------------|----------------|-----------|
| SQLI-001  | SQL Injection via String Concatenation | critical     | security  |
| CRED-001  | Hardcoded Credential Literal           | critical     | security  |
| EXEC-001  | Dangerous OS Command Execution         | high         | security  |
| DESER-001 | Unsafe Deserialization                 | high         | security  |

### SQLI-001 — SQL Injection via String Concatenation

Detects lines where a SQL keyword (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`,
`MERGE`) in a string literal is combined with a `+` concatenation operator.
Severity is elevated to `critical` when a `Statement.executeQuery/execute`
call is also present on the same line.

**False-positive risk**: ORM HQL/JPQL strings that happen to use
concatenation may trigger this rule. Verify that the concatenated values
originate from untrusted input before treating as confirmed.

### CRED-001 — Hardcoded Credential Literal

Detects string literals assigned to identifiers named `password`, `passwd`,
`secret`, `api_key`, `apikey`, `token`, `authtoken`, `access_key`, or
`private_key`.

**False-positive reduction**:
- Empty strings are ignored (placeholders).
- Common placeholder words (`changeme`, `example`, `placeholder`, etc.)
  are ignored.
- Spring/config property substitution patterns (`${...}`) are ignored.
- `System.getenv(...)` calls are not flagged.
- Pure comment lines are skipped.
- Test files (`*Test.java`, `*Tests.java`) produce `low` severity instead
  of `critical`.

### EXEC-001 — Dangerous OS Command Execution

Detects `Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)` and `new ProcessBuilder(...).start()`
calls.  Severity is `high` when string concatenation is present in the same
line (indicating a potentially dynamic/user-controlled command); otherwise
`medium`.

### DESER-001 — Unsafe Deserialization

Detects `new ObjectInputStream(...)`, `.readObject()`, `.readUnshared()`,
XStream's `fromXML(...)`, and `SerializationUtils.deserialize(...)`.
Severity is `high` when a network/request stream reference is on the same
line; otherwise `medium`.

---

## Diff Parsing

The `DiffParser` parses standard unified diff format (output of `git diff`)
and extracts:
- **File path** from `+++ b/...` headers (git prefix `b/` is stripped).
- **Line number** from `@@ -a,b +c,d @@` hunk headers; the target line
  counter is incremented for each added or context line, and held steady
  for removed lines.

If the submitted input is raw code rather than a proper unified diff (no
`+++` header), file is reported as `unknown` and line as `0`.

---

## Limitations

1. **Line-by-line only**: multi-line patterns (e.g. a SQL query built
   across three lines) are not detected unless each individual line
   contains enough of the pattern.
2. **No data-flow**: the engine cannot determine whether a concatenated
   value actually originates from user input.
3. **Java-centric**: rules are written with Java syntax in mind but will
   also match similar patterns in Kotlin, Groovy, and Scala.
4. **No framework awareness**: Spring Data JPA `@Query` with concatenation
   may produce a false positive for SQLI-001.
5. **Regex, not AST**: no abstract syntax tree is built. Patterns may
   produce false positives on unusual formatting.
6. **Historical data**: the engine does not retroactively rewrite findings
   from previous reviews. The recovered historical review (ID 1) retains
   its original findings.

---

## Running the Tests

```bash
# From the project root (thirdeye-backend)
.\mvnw.cmd test
```

Unit tests are in:
- `src/test/java/com/thirdeye/backend/analysis/StaticAnalysisEngineTest.java`
  — pure in-memory tests, no database, no Spring context.
- `src/test/java/com/thirdeye/backend/ThirdeyeBackendApplicationTests.java`
  — Spring Boot integration tests using an isolated H2 in-memory database.

---

## Adding a New Rule

1. Create a class in `com.thirdeye.backend.analysis.rules` that implements
   `AnalysisRule`.
2. Implement `ruleId()`, `name()`, and `analyze(List<DiffLine>)`.
3. Add an instance to the `rules` list in `StaticAnalysisEngine`'s
   constructor.
4. Add unit tests covering at least: one positive detection, one negative
   case, and one false-positive guard.

---

## Testing the Feature Locally

### Sample diff with SQL injection + hardcoded credential

```
--- a/UserService.java
+++ b/UserService.java
@@ -0,0 +1,6 @@
+Connection conn = DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:mysql://localhost/db", "root", "mysecret");
+Statement stmt = conn.createStatement();
+String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + username + "' AND pass='" + password + "'";
+ResultSet rs = stmt.executeQuery(query);
```

### Steps

1. Start the backend: `.\mvnw.cmd spring-boot:run`
2. Start the frontend: `npm run dev` (from `thirdeye-ai-frontend`)
3. Open `http://localhost:5173` → select a project → **Code diff** page
4. Paste the sample diff above in the diff text area, enter a title, click
   **Submit for review**
5. Navigate to **Overview** — status will change from `PENDING` → `ANALYZING`
   → `COMPLETED` (auto-refreshes every 3 seconds)
6. Navigate to **Findings** — you should see:
   - One `critical` or `high` security finding for the `SQLI-001` SQL
     injection pattern
   - One `critical` security finding for the `CRED-001` hardcoded credential
     (`"mysecret"`)
7. Verify file attribution: both findings should report
   `file = UserService.java`

### Verification via API

```bash
# List reviews for project 2 (Lost & Found)
curl http://localhost:8080/api/projects/2/reviews

# Get findings for the new review (replace {id} with actual review ID)
curl http://localhost:8080/api/reviews/{id}/findings

# Get severity summary
curl http://localhost:8080/api/reviews/{id}/findings/summary
```

### Verify historical data is intact

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/api/reviews/1/findings
# Should return the original recovered finding: "No test changes detected in diff"
```

+# ThirdEye AI — Static Analysis Engine (Milestone 1)
+
+## Overview
+
+Milestone 1 replaces the previous mock/placeholder analysis pipeline with a
+genuine deterministic static-analysis engine.  The engine examines the
+**added lines** of a submitted unified diff using a set of pattern-matching
+rules and produces findings that are persisted through the existing
+`Finding` entity and REST API.
+
+**What this is NOT**:
+- Not an AI or LLM model. No external API calls are made.
+- Not a full compiler, parser, or data-flow analyser.
+- Does not perform type inference, cross-file analysis, or interprocedural
+  taint tracking.
+
+A finding means a pattern matched — it indicates a **potential** issue, not
+a confirmed exploitable vulnerability.  Each finding includes the rule ID so
+results are traceable.
+
+---
+
+## Architecture
+
+```
+ReviewController
+    └─> ReviewService.createReview / triggerAnalysis
+            └─> MockAnalysisService.analyzeAsync  (@Async)
+                    └─> StaticAnalysisEngine.analyze(review, diff)
+                            ├─> DiffParser.parse(diff)  → List<DiffLine>
+                            ├─> SqlInjectionRule.analyze(lines)
+                            ├─> HardcodedCredentialRule.analyze(lines)
+                            ├─> DangerousExecutionRule.analyze(lines)
+                            └─> UnsafeDeserializationRule.analyze(lines)
+                    └─> FindingRepository.saveAll(findings)
+```
+
+All new code lives in `com.thirdeye.backend.analysis` and its `rules`
+sub-package.  No existing entities, repositories, controllers, or DTOs
+were changed.
+
+---
+
+## Supported Rules
+
+| Rule ID   | Title                                | Severity (max) | Category  |
+|-----------|--------------------------------------|----------------|-----------|
+| SQLI-001  | SQL Injection via String Concatenation | critical     | security  |
+| CRED-001  | Hardcoded Credential Literal           | critical     | security  |
+| EXEC-001  | Dangerous OS Command Execution         | high         | security  |
+| DESER-001 | Unsafe Deserialization                 | high         | security  |
+
+### SQLI-001 — SQL Injection via String Concatenation
+
+Detects lines where a SQL keyword (`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`,
+`MERGE`) in a string literal is combined with a `+` concatenation operator.
+Severity is elevated to `critical` when a `Statement.executeQuery/execute`
+call is also present on the same line.
+
+**False-positive risk**: ORM HQL/JPQL strings that happen to use
+concatenation may trigger this rule. Verify that the concatenated values
+originate from untrusted input before treating as confirmed.
+
+### CRED-001 — Hardcoded Credential Literal
+
+Detects string literals assigned to identifiers named `password`, `passwd`,
+`secret`, `api_key`, `apikey`, `token`, `authtoken`, `access_key`, or
+`private_key`.
+
+**False-positive reduction**:
+- Empty strings are ignored (placeholders).
+- Common placeholder words (`changeme`, `example`, `placeholder`, etc.)
+  are ignored.
+- Spring/config property substitution patterns (`${...}`) are ignored.
+- `System.getenv(...)` calls are not flagged.
+- Pure comment lines are skipped.
+- Test files (`*Test.java`, `*Tests.java`) produce `low` severity instead
+  of `critical`.
+
+### EXEC-001 — Dangerous OS Command Execution
+
+Detects `Runtime.getRuntime().exec(...)` and `new ProcessBuilder(...).start()`
+calls.  Severity is `high` when string concatenation is present in the same
+line (indicating a potentially dynamic/user-controlled command); otherwise
+`medium`.
+
+### DESER-001 — Unsafe Deserialization
+
+Detects `new ObjectInputStream(...)`, `.readObject()`, `.readUnshared()`,
+XStream's `fromXML(...)`, and `SerializationUtils.deserialize(...)`.
+Severity is `high` when a network/request stream reference is on the same
+line; otherwise `medium`.
+
+---
+
+## Diff Parsing
+
+The `DiffParser` parses standard unified diff format (output of `git diff`)
+and extracts:
+- **File path** from `+++ b/...` headers (git prefix `b/` is stripped).
+- **Line number** from `@@ -a,b +c,d @@` hunk headers; the target line
+  counter is incremented for each added or context line, and held steady
+  for removed lines.
+
+If the submitted input is raw code rather than a proper unified diff (no
+`+++` header), file is reported as `unknown` and line as `0`.
+
+---
+
+## Limitations
+
+1. **Line-by-line only**: multi-line patterns (e.g. a SQL query built
+   across three lines) are not detected unless each individual line
+   contains enough of the pattern.
+2. **No data-flow**: the engine cannot determine whether a concatenated
+   value actually originates from user input.
+3. **Java-centric**: rules are written with Java syntax in mind but will
+   also match similar patterns in Kotlin, Groovy, and Scala.
+4. **No framework awareness**: Spring Data JPA `@Query` with concatenation
+   may produce a false positive for SQLI-001.
+5. **Regex, not AST**: no abstract syntax tree is built. Patterns may
+   produce false positives on unusual formatting.
+6. **Historical data**: the engine does not retroactively rewrite findings
+   from previous reviews. The recovered historical review (ID 1) retains
+   its original findings.
+
+---
+
+## Running the Tests
+
+```bash
+# From the project root (thirdeye-backend)
+.\mvnw.cmd test
+```
+

+- `src/test/java/com/thirdeye/backend/analysis/StaticAnalysisEngineTest.java`

Now I have full context. Here's the design:

**What we can do deterministically** (no AI required):
- For each rule finding, we know: **rule ID, file, line number, what was detected, severity**
- From the finding's `description` we can extract the **evidence snippet** (the actual code)
- We generate Java unit tests using **JUnit 5 / Spring MockMvc** for the specific vulnerability patterns our 4 rules detect
- Tests are honest: they describe what **must be validated**, include the actual offending code as a comment, and are marked `NOT_RUN` (not PENDING/PASSED)
- The `NOT_RUN` status makes it explicit these were never executed

**Schema change needed**: Add `testType` column to `generated_tests` to label each test. The entity already has a `testCode` column (length 10000). No breaking changes — just `ddl-auto=update` will add the column.
